Article Title: ‘It’s madness’: Anand loses on time after declining draw against Sindarov; 20-year-old calls legend ‘world-class’
Article Text:

BENGALURU: Viswanathan Anand ’s difficult start to the 2026 Global Chess League took another turn for the worse on Tuesday as the five-time world champion suffered two defeats in a day, the second coming in painful fashion against 20-year-old Javokhir Sindarov.Playing for Alaskan Knights, Anand had already endured a tough Monday, losing on time to World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen before holding Triveni Continental Kings’ Alireza Firouzja to a draw. Tuesday brought little relief. Anand first resigned against Ian Nepomniachtchi earlier in the day and then, in the evening, ran out of time against Sindarov despite having chances to win.The defeat was particularly frustrating because Anand, playing White, had held the advantage at one stage. With the clock becoming an increasingly important factor in this rapid format, however, the veteran struggled to keep control of the position.To make matters worse, Sindarov had offered a draw. Anand declined, believing he could still press for a win.“It’s just a comedy of errors. He offered a draw when he played 43...Re4+. But it seemed to me that his pieces had no coordination, so I tried to play for win,” Anand, visibly devastated after the loss on time, told reporters.“And then, it’s madness. I think even at the very end, I must have had a draw, but I went with 70.Kxd4+. I already blundered allowing 73.Rf8...Rc4+, and I can’t take on B4,” he explained.Asked what was going wrong for him, Anand could offer little explanation. “I don’t know. If I knew, I would do something,” he remarked.Sindarov, who is preparing to challenge for the world championship later this year, was hardly delighted with his own performance despite securing the crucial win.“Yeah, general happy with the performance but not happy with the game. But, I mean, in the opening, I played very well, but then, like, I made big mistake. I start thinking for five minutes to find the best moves, but in this time control, it’s always hard to find all the best moves,” he said.Sindarov confirmed that he had offered Anand a draw and admitted he was relieved when the Indian legend declined.“I saw the screen. I was just hoping, like, my draw will be, I mean, not so bad. But then I saw they’re just losing, and I was very happy when he didn’t accept my draw. And I was thinking, ‘Okay, I need to go all in, like, I will win or lose.’”With both players reduced to mere seconds, Sindarov felt Anand’s dwindling clock gave him a psychological edge.“I started to understand he felt a little bit nervous when his time was going to less than one minute, and then, somehow, I took this psychological advantage, and I started trying to push, and he missed my last trick,” he said.Despite beating Anand twice in two games, Sindarov played down any suggestion that he has a particular edge over the legend. "No. I mean, I’m just so lucky to win both games,” he added. “It’s very good to play against Anand always, getting, you know, practice against a world champion.”And when asked how highly he rated Anand at 56, Sindarov was full of praise: “He’s world-class," He said. "There are only a few players who can play at this level so close to 60 years old. So, that’s why he was one of the best.”The day started with Ganges Grandmasters beating Alaskan Knights 12-8. American Grandmaster Abhimanyu Mishra’s game against Leon Luke Mendonca ended in controversy after an illegal move and confusion over the clock cost Mishra a likely win.Mumba Masters defeated American Gambits 11-6 in the second match of the day. Triveni Continental Kings beat Pipers 10-4. The much-anticipated clash between Magnus Carlsen and Alireza Firouzja ended in a draw, but the Continental Kings picked up wins on other boards.Before the fourth edition began, Carlsen had joked that he wanted to “flag the s*** out of Alireza Firouzja”. He did not get his wish, but their game drew plenty of attention, with the arena filling up as the evening progressed.In the final match of the day, Anand's Alaskan Knights then went down to American Gambits 9-12.
Article Summary: Viswanathan Anand loses on time to Javokhir Sindarov at 2026 Global Chess League. Five-time world champion had chances to win but ran out of time. Sindarov, 20, is preparing to challenge for world championship later this year.

Article Title: India's New Zealand tour: Over 50,000 tickets sold in just two weeks
Article Text:
Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma (BCCI Photo)

Several matches close to a sell-out

NZC excited by the response

NEW DELHI: The upcoming India tour of New Zealand has already created strong interest among fans, with more than 50,000 tickets sold in just over two weeks.India will tour New Zealand for the first time in six years. The teams will play five T20Is, five ODIs and two Test matches during the tour.The strong ticket sales have given New Zealand Cricket (NZC) a boost ahead of the much-awaited series.Ticket sales opened to the public on Monday after a two-week pre-sale period for Cricket Nation members, Sky customers and ANZ customers.According to a press release: "Ticket sales opened to the public on Monday after a two week pre-sale window for Cricket Nation members, Sky customers, and ANZ customers, with several matches on track to sell out, including the second T20I against India in Christchurch which sits at 75% sold out."Demand has also been high at Eden Park. NZC has opened the stadium's sixth tier of seating for the first time since India's 2019 tour of New Zealand.The upper level will be available for the fourth T20I against India on Friday, October 30."High demand at Eden Park has required the stadium's sixth tier of seating to open for the first time since the 2019 India tour of New Zealand, with the upper level available for the fourth T20I against India on Friday 30 October," the release further stated.NZC Head of Marketing Tim Ellis said the excitement around India's tour was growing."Being able to open up the top level of Eden Park for the first time in years is really exciting and speaks to the swell of excitement building around the tour. Matches at Hagley Oval have always been well attended but to have one of them over three quarters sold already is quite remarkable," Ellis was quoted as saying in the release.Ellis also said NZC was working on several events and activities for fans during the tour."We're deep into planning for a number of events surrounding the tour and have some exciting at-game activations in the works that we're confident will deliver a great experience for fans of all ages," he added.
Article Summary: India will tour New Zealand for the first time in six years. Teams will play five T20Is, five ODIs and two Test matches during the tour. Several matches close to a sell-out, including the second T20I against India in Christchurch which sits at 75% sold out.

Article Title: Dilip Gavit's inspirational journey: From losing his right arm at five after a tree fall to raising the tricolour on podiums
Article Text:
India's para-athlete Dilip Mahadu Gavit celebrates after winning the gold medal at CWG 2026. (PTI photo)

The guru who shaped Gavit's career

The switch from 400m to 100m in Glasgow

India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit, right, gold medallist, and Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath (PTI photo)

'Still a 400m runner'

The laurels he wants next

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: At five, Dilip Mahadu Gavit knew little about the fragility of life. A fall from a tree left him with a serious injury to his right arm, but there was no reason to believe that a childhood accident would alter the course of his life. The wound initially appeared manageable, but it turned septic. What followed was every parent's nightmare. Doctors had no choice but to amputate his arm.For most, losing an arm at such a tender age could have meant the end of dreams before they had even begun. For Gavit, it became the beginning of a battle he would spend years fighting, one that would eventually take him to a place few could have imagined: the Commonwealth Games podium. Earlier this year in Glasgow, the 23-year-old won gold in the men's 100m T47 final in 10.71 seconds, a Commonwealth Games record, and became the first Indian male para-athlete to win gold at the Games.For Gavit, though, the medal's significance ran deeper than the timing or the record. He credited his medal to Vaijnath Kale, the coach who spotted Gavit's potential when he was still a boy competing in local races in Maharashtra."The first thing that comes to my mind is that the day of my event was Guru Purnima . So, in a way, I gave my guru his gurudakshina that day. That makes me feel very good, and it is something I will always remember," Gavit told TimesofIndia.com on the sidelines of an event organised by (SBI) Life Insurance.Gavit's CWG final was no textbook 100m victory. His start wasn't the strongest, and by halfway, he looked to be chasing the race rather than controlling it. The explosive runners had established their advantage, while Gavit leaned on qualities built through years of 400m training. As others began to lose momentum, Gavit kept coming. His speed endurance became his advantage. He ate into the gap in the final 40 metres, moved past the runners ahead of him and crossed the line in 10.71 seconds. The Commonwealth Games record was gone, and so was any doubt about whether a 400m athlete could make a serious impact over 100m.For Gavit, it also vindicated the decision to pursue the event after the 400m was left off the programme. Even after producing the biggest 100m performance of his career, though, he knows there's still work to do.Gavit grew up in Tora Dongri, a tribal hamlet in Nashik, where sporting infrastructure was scarce and opportunities were limited. Gavit used to compete in races at school even when facilities and resources weren't readily available, and his willingness to compete eventually brought him to Kale's attention. Kale, a corporate employee turned coach, was impressed with Gavit and requested his parents to let him train, but due to the family's financial difficulties, he didn't get the green light. Kale was confident that he had found a special talent, and he virtually adopted Dilip.What followed was more than a conventional coach-athlete relationship. Kale took Gavit into his home and gave him the environment he needed to pursue athletics. For a boy from a village with little access to sport, it changed the trajectory of his life. Gavit has never forgotten it."I come from a small village where there aren't many facilities, especially when it comes to sport. To take me from there and keep me at his home is something not many people would do. He did that for me. For me, he has been like God," he reminisced.Kale began moulding him primarily as a 400m runner, an event that demands far more than raw speed. A successful one-lap athlete has to understand pace, conserve energy through the middle stages, and still have enough left to attack the final 100m.Gavit's progress soon took him beyond para-athletics. Gavit competed in open competitions, regularly holding his own against able-bodied athletes. He reached the Under-20 400m final at the open nationals in 2021 and was part of Maharashtra's bronze-medal 4x400m relay team at the 2022 Khelo India Youth Games.His move into international para-athletics took him to the 2022 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou, where he won 400m gold, establishing him as one of India's leading para sprinters. Glasgow would require something different, and interestingly, he did not arrive at the 2026 Commonwealth Games as a 100m specialist. If one event defined the youngster, it was the 400m.On a wet track in Glasgow, though, it was the shortest sprint that gave him the biggest moment of his career. He wasn't among the leaders for much of the race. The pure sprinters' explosiveness had put him behind early, but things changed in the closing stages. Drawing on the speed endurance he has built as a 400m runner, Gavit surged through the final stretch and swept past his rivals.The absence of the 400m from the Commonwealth Games programme left Gavit with a choice. Rather than miss the Games altogether, he turned to the 100m, an event he was already running as part of his preparation for the longer sprint. The shift wasn't as sudden as it may have looked from outside. Kale had been preparing him for the 100m for years."The preparation for the 100m did not start this year. It has actually been going on for the last four years," Kale told this website. "As you saw, he competed in the 100m at the 2023 Asian Para Games in Hangzhou. He reached the quarter-finals and semi-finals, but unfortunately, he fouled in the final and was disqualified."That foul stayed with Gavit. He'd already won a 400m medal at those Asian Games, but the 100m disappointment bothered him. "My coach had actually started preparing me for the 100m much earlier, in 2022. At the Asian Games, I fouled in the 100m, so I could not finish the event. I won a medal in the 400m there, but I still felt bad about the 100m because of the foul," he said.That made Glasgow personal. "So when I won the Commonwealth Games gold in the 100m, it felt really good," he added.There was a practical reason for the switch too. "We have been training for both events in parallel. Since the 400m was not part of the Commonwealth Games programme, we focused on qualifying for and competing in the 100m," Kale explained.The irony of Gavit's CWG triumph is that despite winning one of the most prestigious sprint titles in Indian para-athletics, Kale doesn't see him as a 100m specialist. "He is still primarily a 400m athlete. But his performance in the 100m has also been very good," Kale said.The 100m and 400m are both sprint events, but the demands differ fundamentally: one is a battle for explosive acceleration and maximum velocity, while the other is about combining speed with the ability to sustain it over an entire lap."The 100m is a sprint and demands speed, while the 400m is a speed-endurance event. Balancing the two is quite difficult, but fortunately, we have been managing both very well, and the results have also been very good."Gavit sees the difference clearly himself. "In the 400m, the focus is much greater because you have to plan the entire race. You have to know how to run the first 100m, how to maintain your pace through the middle of the race and then give everything you have in the final stretch," he said."In the 100m, you just have to run hard and the race is over quickly. I actually enjoy the 100m because it finishes so quickly."There's something amusing in that: the athlete who has just conquered the Commonwealth 100m is still happiest thinking of himself as a 400m runner, while his coach tries to make sure both versions of Gavit keep developing.Gavit believes the Glasgow conditions cost him something. "The climate there was not very good, and because of that, my start was a little slow. That is something I want to improve."A Commonwealth gold and a Games record might have been enough for most athletes to sit back and enjoy. Gavit is already looking at the next benchmark. "I want to break the Commonwealth Games record again in 2030."Before then comes a more immediate challenge. The Asian Para Games in Aichi-Nagoya will demand that Gavit quickly switch gears from 100m preparation back to the 400m, and after two months of concentrating heavily on the shorter sprint, Kale knows the transition won't be straightforward."It is definitely a little difficult at the moment because our entire focus has been on the 100m for the last two months. Now, suddenly, we have to shift our focus back towards the 400m. So there are some challenges." But the target is clear. "There is no doubt that we will give our best, and our commitment will be to win medals for India in both events."Gavit wants more than medals. He wants gold in both. "At the next Asian Games, I want to compete in both the 100m and 400m and win gold in both."
Article Summary: Dilip Mahadu Gavit is the first Indian male para-athlete to win gold at the Commonwealth Games. The 23-year-old won gold in the men's 100m T47 final in 10.71 seconds, a Commonwealth Games record. He credits his medal to Vaijnath Kale, the coach who spotted his potential.

Article Title: Hockey Junior Asia Cup: Captain Anmol Ikka scores six goals as India demolish Chinese Taipei 15-0 to reach semifinals
Article Text:
Photo credit: X/@TheHockeyIndia

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Captain Anmol Ikka scored six goals as defending champions India ended their pool-stage campaign with a 15-0 win over Chinese Taipei to reach the semifinals of the men's Junior Asia Cup hockey tournament in Moqi, China, on Wednesday.Anmol scored all six of his goals from penalty corners as India recovered from a goalless first quarter and took complete control of the match over the remaining three quarters.India finished on top of Pool A with 10 points from three wins and a draw. South Korea also reached the semifinals from the group after beating Japan 3-2 to finish second with nine points.Japan, Indonesia and Chinese Taipei were knocked out of the title race and will now play classification matches.India dominated possession in the opening quarter but could not score against a disciplined Chinese Taipei defence.Coach Frederic Soyez used the first-quarter break to ask for more intensity, and India responded immediately.Aryan Xess opened the scoring in the 17th minute before Prabhdeep Singh doubled the lead a minute later. Gursewak Singh added India's third goal in the 22nd minute, with the team scoring three goals in five minutes.Anmol then started his scoring run. He converted a penalty corner in the 25th minute for his first goal. Arjun Santosh Hargude made it 5-0 in the 28th minute before Anmol scored again from another penalty corner in the 29th minute.India went into half-time with a 6-0 lead.The defending champions continued attacking after the break and earned two penalty corners within the first three minutes of the third quarter.Anmol converted both chances to complete his hat-trick and then added another penalty corner goal to take his tally to four.Ajeet Yadav scored India's ninth goal in the 35th minute after another attacking move.Anmol was not done yet. He converted another penalty corner in the 45th minute to score his fifth goal of the match as India ended the third quarter with a 10-0 lead.India continued scoring in the final quarter. Harpal scored a field goal in the 48th minute before Anmol converted his sixth penalty corner in the 51st minute.Harpal added his second goal of the match, while Aryan Xess also completed a brace as India finished with a 15-0 victory and sealed a place in the semifinals.
Article Summary: Defending champions India beat Chinese Taipei 15-0 to reach semifinals. Captain Anmol Ikka scored six goals from penalty corners. India finished on top of Pool A with 10 points from three wins and a draw. South Korea also reached the semifinals after beating Japan 3-2.

Article Title: PT Usha-led IOA forms panel to probe sexual harassment allegations against Hockey India secretary
Article Text:
Asunta Lakra

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The Indian Olympic Association (IOA) has formed a four-member independent inquiry committee to investigate the sexual harassment allegations made against Hockey India secretary Bhola Nath Singh by former India women's hockey captain Asunta Lakra.The committee has been set up following a directive from the Union sports ministry. It will be headed by retired high court judge Deepa Sharma, with former track and field athlete Vandana Rao, former India women's hockey captain Mamta Kharb, and lawyer Sitwat Nabi as members.Lakra, who is also a member of Hockey India's Executive Board, has accused Singh of threatening and harassing her after she objected to the alleged sexual harassment of girls in Jharkhand by local coach Sudhir Golla.The IOA has directed Hockey India to bear all expenses related to the inquiry committee, including honorarium, travel, accommodation and other incidental costs."Hockey India is also requested to extend its full cooperation to the committee and to ensure that all relevant documents, information and such other assistance as may be required is made available to the committee in a timely manner...," IOA president PT Usha's letter to Hockey India stated, as quoted by news agency PTI.The dispute between Lakra and Hockey India has also led to a separate inquiry by the federation's ethics committee.Hockey India's ethics committee issued a show-cause notice to Lakra and started an inquiry after young player Albela Rani Toppo accused the former captain of threatening and intimidating her. Toppo, who is also from Jharkhand, alleged that Lakra threatened to end her career for unspecified reasons.Lakra rejected Hockey India's action and called it "continued intimidation and retaliation". She appealed to sports minister Mansukh Mandaviya to intervene and stop the ethics committee inquiry against her.The sports ministry had earlier asked the IOA to set up an independent panel to investigate Lakra's allegations of sexual harassment against the Hockey India secretary.
Article Summary: Former India women's hockey captain Asunta Lakra has accused Hockey India secretary Bhola Nath Singh of sexual harassment. The committee has been set up following a directive from the Union sports ministry. The IOA has directed Hockey India to bear all expenses related to the inquiry committee, including honorarium, travel, accommodation and other incidental costs.

Article Title: Frances Tiafoe storms back from two sets down to stun Michelsen, reach US Open semis
Article Text:
Frances Tiafoe (Image credit: X)

‘I definitely waited for the last minute’

Michelsen lets Tiafoe back into the match

Tiafoe keeps fighting in the fifth

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Tiafoe makes more history

Frances Tiafoe came back from two sets down to beat Alex Michelsen 5-7, 3-6, 7-5, 6-3, 7-6 (10-6) on Tuesday and reach the US Open semifinals. Tiafoe also trailed 3-0 in the fifth set but fought back once again. He finally won the match after 4 hours, 38 minutes.After the match, Tiafoe went to the other side of the net and hugged Michelsen, who cried on his shoulder after a painful end to his first Grand Slam quarterfinal.Tiafoe admitted he made a poor start to the match and struggled to find his rhythm.“It wasn’t good, let’s put it that way. It wasn’t good,” he said. “Three out of five is a blessing, because you have time to get it together. I definitely waited for the last minute.”The No. 11 seed has now reached the US Open semifinals for the third time. He also made the last four in 2022 and 2024.Tiafoe will face the winner of the quarterfinal between defending champion Carlos Alcaraz and No. 8 seed Ben Shelton.Michelsen looked in control after winning the first two sets. He also led 3-0 in the fifth and looked close to reaching his first Grand Slam semifinal.But Tiafoe refused to give up.Michelsen was serving for the match at 5-4 in the third set when he made two straight double faults. Tiafoe eventually broke after Michelsen failed to finish a shot at the net.“I feel the first three sets I was on top of him. I feel like he didn’t really — he wasn’t playing like Frances. Then I kind of let him back in at 5-4,” Michelsen said. “Then after that, he was playing like Frances does on Ashe. After that, it was a dogfight.”Tiafoe then won the third set and levelled the match by taking the fourth.Michelsen again put Tiafoe under pressure in the deciding set, breaking early to take a 3-0 lead. Tiafoe became frustrated at one point and smashed his racket on the court. But he recovered once again. In the match tiebreak, Tiafoe won three straight points to move 7-4 ahead. Michelsen won the next two points, but Tiafoe responded with a 135 mph ace and took control again.Tiafoe eventually completed the comeback after four hours and 38 minutes.Tiafoe has now joined Andre Agassi as the only American men to reach three US Open semifinals this century. He will also return to the top 10 in the next rankings for the first time in three years. Michelsen, ranked No. 46, fell to 0-6 in matches that go to a fifth set.Tiafoe will now wait for the winner of Alcaraz and Shelton. He plans to watch the match.“I’m going to enjoy this one, though. Let’s go!” he told the crowd in Arthur Ashe Stadium.
Article Summary: Frances Tiafoe came back from two sets down to beat Alex Michelsen. The No. 11 seed has now reached the US Open semifinals for the third time. He will now face the winner of the quarterfinal between Carlos Alcaraz and No. 8 seed Ben Shelton.

MUMBAI: Off-spinning allrounder Washington Sundar, who missed the two-Test series in Sri Lanka due to a hamstring injury, has been cleared to play in India's upcoming three-match T20I series against Afghanistan in New Delhi, TOI has learnt.However, team management and selectors are still awaiting fitness updates on pacer Jasprit Bumrah and seam-bowling allrounders Harshit Rana and Nitish Kumar Reddy, who were picked for the series subject to clearing their fitness tests."Sundar was cleared by the BCCI's medical team after his fitness test, which included a match simulation exercise, at the BCCI Centre of Excellence in Bengaluru on Sept 4. Bumrah, Rana and Reddy underwent their first match simulation on Monday and will undergo their second on Wednesday at the CoE. After that, the CoE will provide a fitness report on the trio," a source tracking developments told TOI. This means a final update on India's squad could come just four days before the first match of the series. Sundar's availability, nevertheless, is a boost for India, who now await clarity on the other three players.Bumrah was ruled out of the Test series in Sri Lanka due to an on-field knee injury sustained during India's white-ball tour of England.Rana suffered a hamstring injury during the England tour in July, while Reddy missed both the UK and Sri Lanka tours due to a quadriceps injury.India had named a full-strength squad, led by Shreyas Iyer, for the three-match T20I series against Afghanistan, with star allrounder Hardik Pandya the notable absentee as he continues to recover from injury. It is almost the same squad that will travel to Japan for the Asian Games.
Article Summary: Washington Sundar has been cleared to play in India's upcoming T20I series against Afghanistan. Team management and selectors are still awaiting fitness updates on Jasprit Bumrah, Harshit Rana and Nitish Kumar Reddy. India had named a full-strength squad, led by Shreyas Iyer, for the three-match series.

Article Title: International Olympic Committee sticks to age cap at 70 for Indian Olympic Association
Article Text:
IOA president PT Usha

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has not approved any relaxation beyond the 70-year age ceiling for candidates contesting or seeking nominations in Indian Olympic Association (IOA) elections.IOA's existing Article 14.3 allows members above 70 to contest if permitted by international charters and statutes.The amended provision, adopted here at Tuesday's Special General Body Meeting (SGBM), removes that exception and fixes 70 as the ceiling for office-bearers and executive council (EC) members."The IOC has said the age cap is 70 years. Accordingly, the IOA constitution has been amended," an IOA official confirmed to TOI.The SGBM, attended by IOA officials, national sports federations (NSFs) and Olympic associations (SOAs), adopted the amended constitution before it goes to the General Assembly for ratification.The changes permit office-bearers or EC members to serve three consecutive terms in position, separately or in combination, before a cooling-off period. Presidential and treasurer term limits remain three and two terms respectively.No election dates to IOA were announced at the SGBM.
Article Summary: IOA's existing Article 14.3 allows members above 70 to contest if permitted by international charters and statutes. The amended provision, adopted here at Tuesday's Special General Body Meeting (SGBM), removes that exception and fixes 70 as the ceiling for office-bearers and executive council members.

Article Title: EPL demands a different kind of intensity: Alexander Isak
Article Text:
Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Alexander Isak believes Liverpool's greatest strength extends beyond tactics or personnel. It lies in the calm authority of captain Virgil van Dijk , Isak told TOI in an interaction facilitated by JioStar. The Swedish striker spoke about adapting to Arne Slot's possession-based system, and now, Andoni Iraola's high-intensity football, returning from injury, and the passion of Liverpool's global fanbase. Excerpts:Liverpool looks like a team in its rebuilding phase. From a striker's perspective, what makes this Liverpool team different from the previous champions?Yes, it's a completely new team with a lot of new players and young players. I don't really know how to explain it. It's just that different players make it a different team.You've now played under Andoni Iraola, who is known for his vertical high-intensity football, as well as Arne Slot, whose approach is more controlled, possession-based. As a striker, what is the biggest adjustment you had to make without the ball?I think for me, it's been about defending in positions where I would be in a good position when we win the ball, ready to attack, ready to counter quickly. So, it's always about thinking where you're at.That spell on the sidelines, did that change the way you watch football? Were you analysing defenders and movements more than when you were actually playing?No, not really. I mean, when I was injured, I didn't watch too much. I followed Liverpool and that was about it. And then I was just doing my rehab.Fans in India stay up late to watch matches. What is your message to them?Of course, we appreciate all support from overseas where we understand that the times are not always very suitable.Hopefully we can do well and have a good season, which makes staying up late more worth it.What has struck you the most about Liverpool as a club?The fans. Their passion and dedication to the club is incredible. Liverpool is a club rich in culture, history, and tradition. It's been really nice to see that up close.You've played in Germany, Spain before you came to England, so how different is the Premier League compared to these other leagues?Every league has its own style and football culture. The Premier League is more physical and faster. Spain is more controlled and technical. There are pros and cons to every league, but the Premier League demands a different kind of intensity.Your captain Virgil van Dijk picked you as the Liverpool player to watch out for this season, so what are your reactions? And what qualities about Van Dijk do you admire the most?I was surprised to hear that. There are so many players in this squad who can have a big season. Hopefully all of us can step up. As for Van Dijk, the thing that stands out most is how calm he is. Whether he's on the ball or defending, he never looks rushed. That calmness spreads through the whole team.(Watch Liverpool vs Fulham in the Premier League 2026-27 on Sept 12, 7:30 PM onwards, LIVE & Exclusive on JioHotstar and Star Sports Network)
Article Summary: Alexander Isak believes Liverpool's greatest strength lies in the calm authority of captain Virgil van Dijk. The Swedish striker spoke about adapting to Arne Slot's possession-based system, and now, Andoni Iraola's high-intensity football.

Article Title: Asian Games host city hit by floods, official says 'we are not worried'

Article Title: 'No one even told us': Linda Noskova questions US Open roof closure delay after loss to Sabalenka
Article Text:
Aryna Sabalenka, of Belarus, returns the ball to Linda Noskova, of the Czech Republic, during the quarterfinal round of the U.S. Open tennis championships, Tuesday, Sept. 8, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo)

Linda Noskova was made to serve as sunlight gave way to shadows during a key stage of her US Open quarterfinal loss to Aryna Sabalenka on Tuesday, after a delay meant the roof above Arthur Ashe Stadium could not finish adjusting in time.Sabalenka was leading 5-4 in the third set when Noskova stepped up to serve. At that point, most of the court was still in sunlight. By the time Noskova played her first point, the shadow had moved close to the middle of the court. After she won that point, almost the entire court was in shade when the next point started.“I did notice the roof closing right after the point, although it started closing even before the point, so it was weird,” Noskova said. "No one even told us about it, I guess. We didn’t expect it at all.“At the same time, I knew that the tournament wanted to keep us in the shade, and not have us play on the light throughout the whole match. But at the same time, it was, like, a crucial point of the match, so I don’t know why they started moving it so late.”The US Open's roof policy states that “the roof may partially close on Arthur Ashe Stadium to move the shade line fully across the court to optimize visibility for players and broadcast.”Since the roof was only being moved enough to create shade and was not being fully closed, the adjustment should have been completed during the changeover before Noskova began serving. However, the process was delayed because the match itself had started late.A full closure of the roof takes about six minutes, meaning play would have to be stopped.After Sabalenka won 7-6 (1), 3-6, 7-6 (10-7), Noskova said the changing shadows had not bothered her.“Well, it was fine the way it was,” the Wimbledon champion said. “I feel like maybe in the very beginning it was more tough than as the match went on, but I don’t know. Didn’t really make a big difference for me if we were playing in shade or not.”

Article Title: Why shouldn’t National Sports Governance Act apply to BCCI, state bodies, asks Supreme Court
Article Text:
BCCI, Supreme Court

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Tired of handling lingering litigations in cricket management for 12 years since it took up and ushered in reforms in the world’s richest cricket organisation, the Supreme Court on Tuesday asked the Board of Control for Cricket in India and state associations why they should not be brought under National Sports Governance (NSG) Act, 2025.With multiple applications by different state cricket associations and their members either for minor changes in their constitution, or disputes arising from factionalism over control over the cash-rich cricket management bodies, a bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana in a cryptic order at the fag-end of the day’s proceedings asked the BCCI and state affiliates why they should not be governed by the NSG Act and sought their responses.The flow of the applications in the original petition filed by BCCI in 2014, which led to framing of its constitution in August 2018 by the SC on the recommendations of Justice R M Lodha committee, continued even after the SC permitted significant amendments to the BCCI constitution in Sept 2022 relating to consecutive terms of the office bearers and cooling off period terms in office.In May this year, the sports ministry notified new rules under the NSG Act to improve management of sports bodies and adjudication of disputes.If the BCCI and state cricket associations agree to be covered under the NSG Act and the Rules framed thereunder, then all the litigation pending before the SC relating to the functioning and management of cricket bodies would get transferred to the sports tribunal, easing a considerable load off the already overburdened SC.NSG Act and Rules mandate a National Sports Board as the central regulatory authority responsible for recognising national sports bodies and monitoring compliance with governance, financial, and ethical standards. These also provide processes for transparent elections and tenure of elected office bearers.
Article Summary: Supreme Court asked the Board of Control for Cricket in India and state associations why they should not be brought under National Sports Governance (NSG) Act, 2025. If BCCI and state cricket associations agree to be covered under the NSG Act and the Rules framed thereunder, then all the litigation pending before the SC would get transferred to the sports tribunal.

CHENNAI: Mohammed Shami and Mukesh Kumar may currently find themselves outside India's red-ball set-up, but the two Bengal pacers offered a timely reminder of their quality on a flat MA Chidambaram Stadium surface on Tuesday.Bowling in Chennai heat, Shami and Mukesh combined for four wickets as East Zone tightened their grip over the Duleep Trophy final. South Zone ended Day Three on 242-6, still trailing by 466 runs after East had posted a mammoth first-innings total.Shami (2-17 in 11 overs) showed superb control as he went on to pick the wickets of well-set Shaikh Rasheed and Smaran Ravichandran, both talented players from the South stable. Mukesh, on the other hand, returned figures of 2-36 from 12 overs. The pair complemented each other beautifully, constantly discussing what length to bowl, and used reverse swing smartly."After roughly 20 overs, there was a little bit of movement - reverse and otherwise. We benefited from that, so we were able to pick up wickets quickly," Mukesh said at the end of day's play.East captain Ishan Kishan was careful with his premier seamers, aware of the physical demands of bowling in humid conditions.Shami opened with a three-over spell that cost just one run, while Mukesh bowled four and removed Ricky Bhui, who edged a delivery that zipped down the leg side to Kumar Kushagra."It is very hot here right now, and the wicket is flat. So, five or six-over spells wouldn't really work here...In fact, long spells can lead to cramps," Mukesh said. "Our plan as a team was to bowl in short bursts...We put in maximum effort into every ball. That worked out well for us."With left-arm spinner Anukul Roy unable to bowl after injuring his bowling hand on Monday, East had to rely on part-time spin.Shikhar Mohan, bowling left-arm orthodox in Anukul's absence, made the most of his opportunity by claiming his maiden first-class wicket when N Jagadeesan (32) sliced a delivery to Abhimanyu Easwaran at backward point.Devdutt Padikkal, fresh from his impressive India performances, reached his half-century off 65 balls but his partnership with Rasheed was broken by Shami. The veteran paceman returned after lunch to dismiss the right-hander, nipping one back sharply to trap him leg-before.Mukesh, also created considerable pressure and picked the prized scalp of Padikkal, who fell for 62. "The plan against Devdutt was to bowl stump-to-stump," Mukesh said. "On wickets like this, if you offer width to batters, runs will leak. Our plan was to stay consistent, bowl dot balls and let them take the risks."The key, Mukesh explained, was not trying to overdo things on a flat pitch. "Speed was a priority, but without fitness you can't increase pace. Then it is about hitting the deck and gauging the length that works on this pitch," he said.Tilak Varma's unbeaten 56 offered South some resistance, with Shreyas Gopal adding 38 before falling to Kounain Quraishi in the last over of the day.East Zone 708 all out. South Zone 242-6 (Padikkal 62, Tilak 56*). Match to continue.

England captain Joe Root has defended Pakistan ahead of the third Test at Edgbaston, saying it is "disrespectful" to claim the visitors have shown "no fight" despite trailing 2-0 in the three-match series.England have already sealed the series after an innings-and-103-run win at Headingley and a 194-run victory at Lord's. Five players without Test experience have been brought into the squad, while Mike Hesson and Ashley Noffke have taken charge for the Edgbaston Test.With Pakistan already out of contention for the series, Babar believes the upheaval can instead give the newcomers a chance to make an impact.“The series is lost but we have nothing to lose,” Babar said on the eve of the Test. “We should play freely and believe in ourselves as a team.”Babar revealed that the sweeping changes came as a surprise to him, with the captain learning about the PCB's decisions only after they had been announced.“It was news to me,” he said. “I found out after.“The PCB decided it, so they will be able to explain better. Article Title: Rajasthan stuck in 2012, Manipur in 2023: How actively are states with CWG medals promoting sports?
Article Text:
Are sports bodies of Indian states promoting the game properly?

Medal tally of India's athletes by birth state/UT

Haryana: Hit on the podium, not so much off it

Manipur still talking about 2023

Rajasthan: 14 years and counting

Uttar Pradesh and Delhi carry the same gloomy picture

And then come Tamil Nadu and others

The ones somewhere in the middle

How active are states/UTs with CWG medallists in promoting sport

Does it matter so much?

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Poll Vote & Share your view What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Social media presence Local sports events Government funding 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

NEW DELHI: Somewhere on a muddy school field in Haryana right now, a teenager is perhaps drilling the same throwing technique over and over, just as she had watched on television just days ago. Her sole aim is to pull off the one like Sharmila Dhankar, India's Commonwealth Games shot put gold medallist.Before the 2026 CWG campaign, she, like many of us, had almost certainly never heard the name. And it's not because Dhankar had not won anything before the Glasgow Games; she had, a gold medal in the Women's Shot Put F57 event at the 2026 Fazza International Para Athletics Championship, but because one of the primary institutions whose entire job was to carry that story back from the medal podium to villages and training grounds across the state has, for all practical purposes, gone quiet.That's the part of this story that rarely gets told. India walked away from Glasgow with 39 medals, and for a week, the athletes who won them were everywhere, garlanded at airports, seated beside ministers, their faces on the evening news. But medals don't build the next generation of athletes by themselves. Somebody has to keep telling their stories, long after the felicitation photo is filed away, to the kid training in a dusty school ground who needs proof that this path actually leads somewhere.We wanted to know which state sports departments are still doing their job of promoting the sports and their grassroots on their social media platforms, and which ones seem to have simply logged off. So we scrolled through the timelines ourselves. Here's what we found.No state produced more glory in Glasgow than Haryana. Eleven medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze, spanning boxing, wrestling, athletics, and para sport, headlined by a Neeraj Chopra silver that will be replayed on sports channels for years.Alongside him were names most of India still had little knowledge of. The likes of Preeti Pawar, Jaismine Lamboria, Sakshi Chaudhary, Priya Ghanghas, Sachin Siwach, and Ankush Panghal, all of whom trained in government facilities, under government schemes, and who'd probably appreciate their own state department cheering as loudly for them as it does for its concert lineups.Because that's the thing. The Sports Department, Government of Haryana's X account has posted exactly once in all of 2026, and it's a flyer for the music acts playing at the Chief Minister's Cup.Facebook and Instagram follow a similar rhythm with a short cluster of posts around that February event, and then not much else.Eleven medals, and not one dedicated post to show for it. Somewhere in Rohtak or Bhiwani, a young pugilist training in Priya Ghanghas's discipline would probably just like a little proof that someone up top is paying attention.Manipur's page has an odd time-capsule quality to it. This is the state that gave India Mirabai Chanu, one of the country's most beloved Olympic medalists, and this Commonwealth Games alone produced four medalists from Manipur, Chanu's gold among them, alongside Rishikanta Singh, Bindyarani Devi, and Jadumani Singh.And yet the Department of Youth Affairs & Sports' X account hasn't posted since October 2023, a "Run for Unity" event, frozen well before any of this year's medals happened.Although the Facebook page has had a few sporadic posts here and there this year, its Instagram account has managed just two posts since January. It’s the kind of gap that makes you wonder if someone simply forgot the login details somewhere along the way.If there's one number in this whole exercise worth sitting with, it's this: the official Sports Department, Government of Rajasthan hasn't posted on Facebook since April 14, 2012.Fourteen years, through Arundhati Choudhary's Commonwealth gold and everything else that's happened in Rajasthan sport since.Its X account's last original post predates a retweet from March 2021, and there's no Instagram at all. A parallel handle, the Rajasthan State Sports Council, exists across all three platforms and is barely livelier.Somewhere behind Choudhary's medal is a genuinely good story, but it just hasn't found a home on the one page built to tell it.Gulveer Singh managed both a silver and a bronze for Uttar Pradesh this Games, a rare double that would make a great centrepiece for the state's sporting year. Instead, across two separate official handles on three platforms, Uttar Pradesh Sports has produced little beyond reposts, while its sister account, Sports Directorate, Govt of Uttar Pradesh, hasn't posted at all in 2026.Delhi Government, for its part, doesn't run a dedicated sports account at all on any of the popular social media platforms, so gold medalist Harsh Singh and bronze medalist Tejaswin Shankar, both representing India's capital, don't really have an institutional cheerleader online, their wins quietly absorbed into the general churn of city government updates. Both athletes are, in effect, doing their own promotional legwork.Set against all that quiet, Tamil Nadu feels like a different sport altogether. Its Sports Tamil Nadu handles post multiple times a day, celebrating not just its own three medalists, Praveen Chithravel, Selva Prabhu, Muthupandi Raja, but athletes from other states too, weaving in government scheme updates without it ever reading like bureaucracy.Every medallist got a dedicated post. Somewhere in Tamil Nadu, a kid training in long jump or wrestling doesn't have to wonder whether the sport leads anywhere. The state tells them, publicly, almost daily.Madhya Pradesh, Chhattisgarh, Karnataka's Facebook and Instagram pages, Assam, Bihar, and Tripura all follow a version of that same habit, active, consistent, generous with attention toward athletes nobody outside their district would otherwise know existed.Kerala doesn't run a separate sports handle on X but keeps its Facebook and Instagram genuinely lively, making sure Murali Sreeshankar and Mohammed Basil's silvers got their due.Andhra Pradesh mirrors that same rhythm across all three platforms.Not every state falls neatly into being inactive or staying proactive. Punjab's account managed just two posts on X all year, New Year's and Republic Day, though its Facebook and Instagram carry a bit more life around coaching and departmental meetings, even if athletes rarely get top billing.Uttarakhand was genuinely active last year before cooling off in 2026, leaning more toward government scheme announcements on Facebook, though its Instagram at least carried two posts around the Games.Maharashtra has dedicated posts up for both Sarvesh Kushare and Dilip Gavit, with Instagram staying fairly regular, enough effort to stay out of the quiet column.Karnataka's X account hasn't posted since March 2024, around an unrelated cultural-team event, even though its Facebook and Instagram have stayed warm and active toward its CWG medalists.It is worth asking why this actually matters, beyond good manners. Well, a state sports department's social media feed isn't just a courtesy board for congratulations; it's one of the cheapest, most direct tools available to build the next generation of athletes.A youngster in a small town is far more likely to pick up a javelin because they saw a state government post celebrating someone from their own district. Even when it comes to promoting any government policy, social media can be as effective.Visibility drives aspiration. There's a funding logic too. Sponsors, corporates, and even state finance departments allocate resources partly based on visible public interest, and a well-run social account is often the easiest evidence a sport has that interest.ALSO READ: Anahat Singh: What is in the name? A word from Guru Nanak's prayer, now India's squash sensation Silence, on the other hand, sends the message that grassroots sport isn't a priority worth the effort of a single post, even when the state has just produced a medallist on the world stage.It is worth it because sometimes, the first step towards building a sporting culture is simply showing people that their achievements are being seen.
Article Summary: India won 39 medals at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. Haryana produced 11 medallists, including seven gold, two silver, two bronze. But the state sports department has posted just once in all of 2026. What do you think is more important for grassroots sports promotion? Government funding or social media presence? Share your view.

NEW DELHI: Boxer Lovlina Borgohain's decision to object to a distorted Indian map during the Commonwealth Games earned special appreciation from Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time.Lovlina, who won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow, was among India's medal winners who interacted with Modi at his residence on Sunday. The meeting, attended by Sports Minister Mansukh Mandaviya, Minister of State for Sports Raksha Khadse and Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha, saw athletes recount their experiences from the Games in an informal and emotional setting.In a little over 10-minute video of the interaction shared by the Prime Minister's Office on Monday, Modi brought up Lovlina's confrontation with a restaurant in Glasgow after she noticed a distorted Indian map.“Kya hua wo restaurant waale se jhagda kar rahi thi? (What happened, you were fighting with that restaurant guy?)” Modi asked.Lovlina laughed before explaining why she intervened.“We had such a good performance and it was the last day of the Games. It was a happy occasion sir, we were celebrating and I didn't like it when I saw the distorted map. I politely told them and they have made the changes also,” she explained.Modi applauded the boxer for noticing the issue despite being in the middle of celebrations after her medal-winning campaign.“To be able to recognise the significance of that map at a time when you were celebrating and the Games were over, I can tell you truthfully, that video was not ordinary. It will be remembered by people for a very long time,” he told the Tokyo Olympics bronze medallist.India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.The interaction also provided an emotional window into Mirabai Chanu's journey to her gold medal in the women's 48kg category. The weightlifter produced a Games-record lift of 190kg, but her triumph came after four difficult years following her one-kilogram miss at the Paris Olympics. Modi asked Mirabai about the tears she shed on the podium and even fed her a laddu during their interaction.“Itne aansu tapak rahe the (So many tears were rolling down),” Modi remarked.Mirabai explained that the tears represented years of accumulated emotions.“I was very happy and emotional at that moment. I was crying because I missed a medal in the Paris Olympics by one kilogram. I have faced a lot in these last four years. I was battling injuries and some family problems too.“There were a lot of things. So, these four years were very tough for me. And when I stood on the podium, our flag went up and the anthem played, it was hard to stop myself,” she said.The meeting also had its lighter moments. Boxer Narender Berwal, who won silver in the +90kg category, recalled a funny exchange with a Pakistani boxer after beating him at the 2015 World Military Games.“During the 2015 World Military Games, I had a bout with a Pakistani boxer. I won it but when we were together in the medical room for treatment to our niggles, he said to me 'Bhaijan aapka naam Narender hai, aapke coach ka naam Narender hai, aapke Pradhan Mantri ka naam Narender hai, mujhe Narender naam se nafrat ho gayi hai.' (Brother, you, your coach and your PM are all named Narender. I hate this name now),” he recalled, drawing laughter from Modi.The Prime Minister also underlined the broader significance of the athletes' achievements, saying their medals were helping inspire a new generation.“I have been in this house for 12-13 years now and if there is one group that I have met regularly here, it is the athletes because of your efforts to win medals for India and your tradition of scaling new heights.“Far more than our push to promote sports in schools, it is your medals that inspire people,” Modi said.
Article Summary: Lovlina Borgohain won silver in the women's 75kg category in Glasgow. Prime Minister Narendra Modi described the moment as one that would be remembered for a long time. India finished fourth in Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 golds, with boxing contributing seven gold medals.

NEW DELHI: “From every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping.”Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an emotional message for Mirabai Chanu as he interacted with India's Commonwealth Games 2026 medal winners at his residence on Sunday, reflecting on the sacrifices behind the country's successful campaign in Glasgow.Modi hosted the medal-winning contingent at 7, Lok Kalyan Marg and heard athletes recount some of the moments that defined their journeys at the Games. India returned from Glasgow with 39 medals, including 13 gold, 17 silver and nine bronze, finishing fourth in the overall standings.During one of the conversations, Modi recalled the emotional scenes surrounding Mirabai's gold-medal triumph.“Tears were falling from you. I feel as if from every drop of tears, gold medals are dripping,” Modi told the Olympic silver medallist.Mirabai, who won gold in Glasgow, opened up about the difficult journey that preceded her Commonwealth Games triumph, including the disappointment of the Paris Olympics.“I was very happy, and emotional too. That day the happiness was greater and I cried because at the Paris Olympics, I lost a medal by 1 kg. In a player’s life what all we have to face. So within these 4 years, how much and what all I had faced, every time injuries were going on and all that was happening.So with great difficulty I had faced these 4 years. So when all that happened, on the podium when I stood, sir, and when our flag goes up and our national anthem plays, sir, we cannot stop, sir, tears come out on their own,” she said.Modi responded by highlighting the wider impact of the athletes' achievements.“This is very good. It is not as if this achievement of yours is considered only your achievement; your victory becomes a very big inspiration for the coming generations.”The informal interaction also saw athletes share lighter and deeply personal moments from their Glasgow campaigns.Modi reminded para shot put gold medallist Sharmila Dhankar of a promise she had made earlier.“You made a promise. Last time, yours, both daughters will become players,” Modi said with a smile.Dhankar replied: “Haanji, right now they are young in age. In the next Commonwealth, one family will bring 3 medals.”Men's 100m T47 gold medallist Dilip Gavit, meanwhile, spoke about dedicating his performance to his guru.“When I was running, when my event was on 29th (July), that day was Guru Purnima, so that day I gave a gift to my guru,” he was heard saying in the video.In another video posted by Modi, gold medallist boxer Sakshi Chaudhary introduced herself and the contingent.“Hello friends! This is Sakshi Chaudhary. Today, our honourable Prime Minister has invited us, the Commonwealth Games medalists, and we feel very proud. We are extremely happy to have met him; he is very humble. Sir, would you like to say something?” she said.Modi replied with a message that summed up his interaction with the athletes: “Jo khelega, woh khilega” (The one who plays, will blossom). “Always cheer for Bharat.”India's fourth-place finish came despite a significantly smaller contingent and a reduced sporting programme compared to Birmingham 2022. India sent 122 athletes to Glasgow, compared to 210 in Birmingham, while 30 of its 61 medals in 2022 came in sports that were not part of the Glasgow programme.Despite those limitations, India retained its fourth-place position and improved its medal conversion rate, with 38 athletes returning home with medals. Long-distance runner Gulveer Singh was the only Indian athlete to win two medals.The Glasgow Games concluded after 11 days, with Scotland handing over the Commonwealth Games flag and ceremonial baton to India ahead of the 2030 edition in Ahmedabad.The symbols were handed to Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, Indian Olympic Association president PT Usha and Gujarat Deputy Chief Minister Harsh Sanghavi during the closing ceremony.Ahmedabad will become only the second Indian city to host the Commonwealth Games after New Delhi staged the 2010 edition.

Article Title: From hospital bed to CWG gold: How Jaismine Lamboria fought the odds in Glasgow
Article Text:
India's Jaismine Lamboria celebrates after winning the women's 57kg boxing final. (AP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Just weeks before stepping into the ring at the Commonwealth Games, Jaismine Lamboria wasn’t thinking about medals. She was searching for answers. The recurring fever had refused to go away.Multiple medical tests showed nothing unusual and the Indian boxer tried to push through, managing the symptoms with paracetamol. When the illness persisted, she was admitted to a hospital in Mohali. Doctors finally diagnosed a bacterial infection, putting her on an intensive 14-day course of medication. For an athlete preparing for one of the biggest competitions of the year, it could easily have been the end of the campaign.Instead, it became the beginning of one of the most remarkable comebacks of her career. “I was avoiding further medical tests because the initial reports were coming back normal. We didn’t know what exactly had to be treated. Finally, after I was admitted, they detected a bacterial infection and I was on medication for 14 days,” the 57kg boxer said.When she was discharged, the clock was already ticking. Barely three weeks remained before the Games.“I started training only on July 1. Initially it was just warm-up, walking and stretching. I had very little time, so we had to be patient.”The physical recovery was only one part of the challenge. During those uncertain weeks, sports psychologist Priya Vrinda became a constant source of support, ensuring the illness didn’t break her confidence.“When I was sick, I was already connected with Priya Vrinda ma’am. She kept me mentally strong and never allowed me to go down,” Jaismine said. That resilience was evident when she returned to competition. Jaismine boxed with maturity, tactical discipline and composure to upgrade the Commonwealth bronze she had won four years ago into gold in the 57kg.One of Jaismine’s biggest assets inside the ring has been her reach in her category. While every opponent may not be shorter — Jaismine stands five feet seven inches in her socks — she believes her physical advantage has become an important weapon thanks to careful coaching. “My coaches taught me how to use my reach properly. It definitely gives me an advantage in many bouts.”
Article Summary: Jaismine Lamboria won gold in the women's 57kg boxing at the Commonwealth Games. The Indian boxer had been suffering from a recurring fever. Doctors diagnosed a bacterial infection and put her on a 14-day course of medication. Jaismine credits her coach Priya Vrinda with helping her recover.

Article Title: How Jadumani Singh's risky weight change nearly derailed his CWG dream before winning Glasgow silver
Article Text:

A bold gamble after the 50kg category disappeared

The selection maze before Glasgow

Jadumani Si​ngh's Road to CWG Silver (AI-generated Infographic)

Jadumani Singh Mandengbam (PTI Photo)

Why the gold slipped away

File Pic: L Sarita Devi (PTI Photo)

Olympic gold remains the ultimate dream

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: When Indian pugilist Jadumani Singh Mandengbam stepped onto the podium to receive the men's 55kg silver medal at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, it marked the culmination of a journey that had almost ended before it had even begun.The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer was one of India's standout performers, winning four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games for the first time.Yet, behind that success lay months of uncertainty, selection hurdles and a weight-category gamble that nearly cost him a place on the flight to Scotland.Speaking exclusively to TimesofIndia.com, former world champion and Jadumani's mentor, Laishram Sarita Devi, recounted how the young boxer refused to abandon his Olympic dream even when every obstacle seemed stacked against him.Jadumani had built his reputation in the 50kg category, winning medals at World Boxing Cups before learning that the division would no longer feature in the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games or Olympic programme.Rather than remain in a non-Olympic category, he decided to move up to 55kg — a division already occupied by some of India's biggest names."He continued to consult with me. Whenever he had to make a big decision, he called up and consulted with me — like increasing his weight category," Sarita told TimesofIndia.com."After he won a World Cup medal in 50kg, he got to know that the weight category is no longer in the CWG, Asian Games and Olympics. He wanted to move to 55kg."The decision immediately brought fresh challenges."Army had their No. 1 boxer in the 55kg category in Pune, who is Services' No. 1 boxer. And the weight category also has Amit Panghal — Olympian and Asian champion. He said he wanted to move up the weight to compete at CWG, Asian Games etc, but was discouraged by hearing questions like whether he would be able to compete at that level, which created a doubt in him," she said.Sarita, however, wanted only one answer: "We sat down and I asked him, 'Are you confident about the decision?' He said he was, so I told him to move up the category."The decision created another problem.Without competing in the National Championships, Jadumani could not enter the national coaching camp. But because he belonged to the Army Sports Institute, Services already had its designated 55kg representative. Attempts to let him represent Manipur also failed."We tried to make him compete for the state of Manipur, but we didn't get an NOC because he is with the Army," Sarita said.Relief finally arrived through a Boxing Federation of India (BFI) policy that granted direct entries to the National Championships for World Boxing Cup medallists. The move was aimed at rewarding elite international performers and ensuring they were not blocked by the usual domestic qualification pathways.The decision allowed Jadumani to compete directly in the 55kg draw despite the institutional overlap, resulting in multiple squad members — Pawan Bartwal, Jadumani Singh and Amit Panghal — finding themselves in the same weight-category draw.Sarita said her ward grabbed the opportunity with both hands."He then got a chance to compete in 55kg in the Nationals. Due to his effort, he won against the Services No.1, Olympians etc to be named Best Boxer in the Nationals. After that he got the chance to be part of the India camp," she said.He then cleared the final selection trials, which included physical assessments alongside ring performances."He participated in the final trial for the CWG and Asian Games — which had many aspects like strength and endurance tests before fighting in the ring. He won all of it to get selected for the CWG and was really happy and started training hard," she added.Just when Glasgow appeared certain, another setback emerged.Because Jadumani had only recently moved into 55kg, he did not possess the Asian ranking required under the Sports Ministry's eligibility criteria for Commonwealth Games selection."He got an explanation mail from the Sports Ministry, which put him in immense tension ahead of the Games," Sarita recalled.Under the ministry's guidelines, boxers were expected to be ranked among Asia's top eight in their respective categories."He was ranked No. 2 in 50kg, but he lacked a ranking in the new 55kg category. He had only competed in one Asian Championship in the new weight category before the trials for CWG and, being new to the category, lost in the quarterfinals," she said.That led to fresh doubts over his selection."He was disheartened when questions were raised whether he was a medal prospect because he was not in the rankings prescribed by the ministry. He called me and said the coaches were saying he may or may not be on the flight to the CWG because of this letter from the ministry," she recalled.The uncertainty only ended after BFI submitted a detailed explanation to the ministry, outlining Jadumani's circumstances following his weight-category switch."BFI replied to the ministry properly, explaining everything and after a lot of effort his ticket to Glasgow was approved. What I like about him is that he is the kind of person who doesn't give up and has a very strong will power," she said.Jadumani eventually reached the final after four demanding contests, each won by an identical 5-0 margin. But Sarita believes the scheduling ultimately worked against him."Jadumani's four bouts were very tough. He played all out in all the bouts till the semifinals as he got proper rest and recovery time. Since the gold medal opponent got a bye earlier, he had fewer bouts than Jadumani," she explained.The semifinal-final turnaround, she felt, proved decisive. There was a one-day gap after every bout until the semifinals, but there was no gap between the semifinal and final in Glasgow."Jadumani fought his semifinal in the evening and got the final bout the next morning only, so he did not get much time for recovery. If it was in the evening, he could have fought better. When he entered the ring for the final, I saw his face and body language sitting here and realised he had not had enough recovery," she said.The experience, she believes, underlines the growing importance of sports science."In such situations, we should look for how we can enhance or speed up the recovery process through sports science. We should discuss it to make sure our boxers can give 100 per cent every time they enter the ring," she added.Sarita first noticed Jadumani as a youngster competing in a local tournament."When I saw Jadumani for the first time, it was a tournament for young boys. His movement was really pleasing and I thought he could become a good boxer in the future. I identified him at that time only and gave him Rs 500 because I was very pleased with his performance," she recalled."Jadumani did not start with me from the grassroots. He learnt his basics from another academy. He came to my academy when he was preparing to enrol in the Army Sports Institute in Pune. At that time, I did not have any infrastructure and was coaching from a makeshift setup. And then Covid happened, we had to train in a very isolated small makeshift place,” she added.Years later, after training together through difficult Covid-19 conditions and watching him overcome one hurdle after another, Sarita believes Glasgow is only the beginning."We missed gold at the CWG, but we will work hard to get gold at the Asian Games for sure," she said.The bigger ambition, however, stretches far beyond continental success."His first and primary target remains Olympic gold. Commonwealth Games and Asian Games are the stepping stones in that journey. He will try to win India's first Olympic gold medal in boxing," Sarita concluded.
Article Summary: Jadumani Singh Mandengbam won silver at the 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow. The 22-year-old Manipuri boxer won four consecutive unanimous 5-0 verdicts to storm into the bantamweight final before settling for silver against Australia's Jye Dixon. His medal also formed part of India's historic boxing campaign, which yielded seven golds and three silvers, making the country the No. 1 boxing nation at the Games.

Article Title: Days after historic CWG gold, Dilip Gavit leaves without meeting Raj Thackeray after two-hour wait
Article Text:
India's Dilip Mahadu Gavit (PTI Photo)

Invited, but left waiting

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

A champion who made history in Glasgow

A journey built on resilience

Just days after scripting history for Indian para athletics at the Commonwealth Games, gold medallist Dilip Gavit found himself making headlines for a very different reason. The 23-year-old sprinter, who became India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event, waited for nearly two hours to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray in Nashik on Thursday before leaving without the meeting taking place.According to Gavit's coach quoted by PTI, Vaijanath Kale, the para-athlete had been invited to meet Thackeray during the MNS chief's visit to Nashik. However, despite arriving at the scheduled venue, Gavit and his coach were made to wait for nearly two hours. A video from the venue showed MNS workers requesting the duo to wait longer while trying to explain that Thackeray was occupied."We were waiting for quite some time... Sir is busy. We will meet him later," Kale is heard saying in the video before they eventually left.The incident came just days after Gavit delivered one of India's biggest moments at the Commonwealth Games. Clocking a Games-record 10.71 seconds, the Nashik sprinter won the men's 100m T47 gold medal, leading a historic Indian one-two finish alongside Mohammed Basil Morssinganakath, who claimed silver. The victory marked India's first-ever Commonwealth Games gold medal in para athletics 100m T47.Gavit's success carries a deeper significance given his remarkable journey. Born into an economically disadvantaged tribal family in Maharashtra, he lost his right arm in a childhood accident. His life changed when coach Vaijanath Kale took him under his wing at the age of 12, supporting his education and athletic development. After winning gold in Glasgow, Gavit emotionally dedicated the medal to Kale, crediting his coach for transforming his life.
Article Summary: Dilip Gavit was invited to meet Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) chief Raj Thackeray. The 23-year-old sprinter waited for nearly two hours for the meeting to take place. The incident came just days after he became India's first Commonwealth Games gold medallist in the men's 100m T47 event.

Article Title: How Harsh fought through pain to script CWG history, now targets Asiad medal
Article Text:
How judoka Harsh overcame pain

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Harsh Singh's right knee still swells. It still hurts. Every time the Indian judoka steps onto the mat, he is reminded of the ACL and meniscus tear that nearly derailed his career. But at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, pain took a back seat as the 23-year-old scripted history by becoming India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist."The pain never really goes away," Singh told TOI in an interview on Thursday. "Sometimes my knee still swells up and feels tight. During the CWG, I felt the pain and the knee occasionally got swollen. After surgery, the joint never became exactly the way it was before. There's always a little discomfort during fights. You have to ignore it and continue. The medal kept me going."The historic triumph came less than a year after Singh tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport (IIS) in Aug 2025. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition."I was in rehabilitation for almost a year. The entire coaching team at the IIS, recovery specialists and Spencer sir (Mackay, S&C expert) helped me throughout.They rebuilt my strength step by step. Because of the IIS and their entire team, I was able to come back on the mat, qualify for the CWG and represent India," he said.The comeback demanded another battle off the mat. Months away from competition saw his weight rise to nearly 72kg, forcing him to shed more than 12kg to return to his 60kg category. Gold at a ranking tournament and bronze at the senior National championships sealed his place in India's CWG squad.Despite lingering discomfort, Singh dominated in Glasgow, with only a hard-fought semifinal stretching him before he clinched the historic title."The semifinal (against the Australian Pedro Carlos) was the toughest. In the 60kg category, even a small point can decide the match. We didn't want to concede anything and stayed aggressive," he recalled.With CWG gold secured, Singh has already shifted his attention to next year's Asian Games. Training stints in Japan and South Korea are part of his preparations as he looks to bridge the gap with Asia's best."I want to improve my speed, grip and strength. Japanese and Korean players are very fast, so training there will help," he said.Born into a modest family, with his father working as a daily-wage labourer, Singh once trained without owning a judo uniform. Support from the govt's schemes and a privately funded athletes' training centre changed the course of his career."My life has changed because of this medal. More people have started noticing judo," he said. "But the best compliment came from my family. They told me, 'You have made the entire family proud.' That meant more than anything else."Having conquered injury to create CWG history, Singh's next aim is clear — turning a gritty comeback into an Asian Games podium finish.
Article Summary: Harsh Singh became India's first-ever men's judo gold medallist. The 23-year-old tore his ACL and meniscus while training at the Inspire Institute of Sport. Surgery followed in Oct last in Bengaluru before a year-long rehabilitation helped him return to competition.

Article Title: 'I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan': Arshad Nadeem blames Glasgow cold for CWG poor show
Article Text:
Arshad Nadeem (AFP Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Lausanne Diamond League next

Pakistan’s Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds, saying the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.Nadeem managed 77.41 metres with his second throw after opening with a foul. His third attempt was 75.39m, leaving him outside the top eight.“The weather was extremely cold and I personally felt that it affected my body. As you have seen in many of my previous competitions, my run-up is usually very smooth, but this time it wasn’t… because my body had become stiff due to the cold conditions. My fitness was good and my health was fine, but ultimately whatever Allah wills is what happens,” he told reporters on Wednesday.Despite the result, Nadeem said he remains determined to make a strong comeback and urged fans to continue supporting him.“Please don’t lose heart and don’t stop supporting me either. Whatever I have achieved has only been possible because Allah blessed me with the opportunity to do it. The respect and recognition Pakistan has received around the world have come through years of hard work. I worked tirelessly while staying in Pakistan,” he added.“God willing, I will prepare with full dedication for the upcoming competitions and once again raise Pakistan’s flag on the international stage.”Nadeem also responded to criticism on social media, saying he understood the disappointment among Pakistani fans.“I have heard many things on social media, but I want everyone to remember that I am Pakistan’s son, and I always will be,” he maintained.Nadeem’s next challenge will be the Lausanne Diamond League in Switzerland on August 21. He will face a strong field that includes India’s Neeraj Chopra , Commonwealth champion Rumesh Tharanga Pathirage, Keshorn Walcott, Anderson Peters and Thomas Rohler.Nadeem will hope to regain his form before the Asian Games later this year.
Article Summary: Olympic javelin champion Arshad Nadeem has blamed the cold Glasgow weather for his disappointing performance at the Commonwealth Games. The defending champion finished ninth after failing to make the final three rounds. He said the low temperature made his body stiff and affected his usually smooth run-up.

Article Title: Glasgow to Ahmedabad: Gujarat receives Commonwealth Games flag as 2030 countdown begins
Article Text:
Neeraj Chopra, left, hands over the Commonwealth Games Federation flag to Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president P T Usha during the closing ceremony of the 23rd Commonwealth Games (CWG), at OVO Hydro, in Glasgow, Scotland. (PTI)
